chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 311 to 320, Othalanthaiyar's paalai decade on the going (செலவுப் பத்து): the man, and in 313 the girl, crosses the wasteland of killing elephants, scorched trees and flaming silk-cotton, and those left behind measure the road by their own wasting, ask whether he will delay or forget, bless the hill that hid him, and find that the heart too has gone and not come back.

311.reading: The woman says her lover has crossed a forest whose road so frightens travellers that even the panchuram call of the girls plucking vengai flowers alarms them, and her heart keeps asking whether he will stay away long.
311.nuance: The fear is put first in the travellers, not in her: a harmless sound from the hill, the flower-pluckers' cry, is enough to startle anyone on that road, so the danger he faces is measured by other people's nerves before she turns to her own worry about delay (நீடுவர் கொல்).

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone across the hard tract and she is left behind

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: நினையும்என் நெஞ்சே gives the woman's own voice; the friend is the likely hearer

312.reading: The woman blesses, again and again, the hill with falls bright as a sword that has hidden her man, strong in the hunt, from her sight, praying it stay full of virtue even if drought comes upon it.
312.nuance: She blesses rather than curses the hill that robbed her of the sight of him: the wish that it keep its virtue (and its water) even in drought is a wish for his safe passage over it. If என்னை is read as 'my father', the speaker would instead be the girl in flight looking back at the hill that hides her home, and the blessing would be for the cover it gives.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill has taken the departing man out of sight, in a land that may dry

comparisons.tenor: the gleam of the hill's waterfall

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the vocative குன்றே makes the hill the addressee; என்னை is taken as 'my man', the one it hid

313.reading: The speaker tells the mother that her daughter's desire is a scorching thing: leaving them wasted with grief, life ebbing and hearts ruined, their beloved girl has crossed the forest of a tract that lies between lands.
313.nuance: தெறுவது, 'that which burns', is said of the girl's love itself, not of the man or the road: the household's grief is laid at the door of her desire, the force that made the forest crossable for her.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has gone through the forest with her lover

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: நும்மகள் (your daughter) is said to the mother by someone of the household, and நம் காதலோள் claims the girl as the speaker's own as well; the foster mother fits best, the friend is possible

314.reading: The woman says they report that the road taken by the man who tired of lying on her shoulders is a long hard waste where ghouls feast with whirling bright bangles, dark-eyed crows and vultures fill the sky, and the small-eyed elephant roams after killing men.
314.nuance: The scene is a battlefield's: ghouls, crows and vultures over men the elephant has killed. தோளிடை முனிநர், 'those who grew weary between our shoulders', turns his going into a rejection of her embrace, so the road of corpses is what he preferred to it.

thinai_evidence.note: the long hard wasteland with its killing elephant is the tract of separation

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: நம் தோளிடை முனிநர் is the woman's complaint about the man; the friend may also be the speaker on her behalf

315.reading: The woman says they report that he is far away and does not hear the outcry of her long eyes, cool as dewy flowers, that have taken to the bed, he who crossed the forest of groves where bamboo grows old, leaving her in a sorrow that undoes what she cherished.
315.nuance: பூசல், an outcry or public clamour, is given to the eyes, so the weeping is imagined as a shout he is too far to hear: her grief is loud and the distance makes it silent.

thinai_evidence.note: he is far beyond the forest and she is left to grieve

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the outcry of the eyes is hers; the friend is the likely hearer

316.reading: The woman says that, letting her golden ornaments and gold-wrought discs fall away and the fine lines of her chariot-broad waist fade, he has surely gone into the forest on the shining mountains where the thin-barked omai stands tall and tigers walk the paths.
316.nuance: The two halves are set as cause and place: the loss of her gold and the fading of her waist-lines happen here, the tiger paths and omai trees are there, and மன்ற ('surely') makes her body the proof that he has gone.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone into the forest and her body wastes

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the ornaments and waist are hers; the friend may be speaking of her

317.reading: The woman asks her friend to come and think with her why her heart, which went to the country of the man who crossed the hard track of the hot paalai forest, burnt bare of all green, has stayed there so long.
317.nuance: The man's delay is restated as the heart's: it is her heart that has gone to his land and lingers (சென்ற நெஞ்சம் நீடிய), so she asks the friend to deliberate about her own absent heart, the one part of her that did make the crossing.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names the hot paalai forest and its hard track

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: she opens with சூழ்கம் வம்மோ தோழி

318.reading: The woman says that the men who crossed the high-peaked mountains of a tract where roaring fire ran have surely killed her longing outright, leaving her chosen beauty pale, hard distress tormenting her, and the bangles slipping from her broad shoulders like bamboo.
318.nuance: நசைநனி கொன்றோர், 'those who utterly killed my longing', names the man as a killer: what dies is not her love but her hope, and the forest fire of line 4 runs through the land he chose over her.

thinai_evidence.note: the men have crossed the mountains and her body pales and wastes

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the pallor and shoulders are hers; the friend is the likely hearer

319.reading: The woman asks whether their lover has crossed the forest of withered trees and cracked earth in a tract scorched by rays that hurt the eyes, and whether he has forgotten them, who do not forget.
319.nuance: The two questions run in parallel (இறந்தனரோ, மறந்தனரோ): crossing the forest and forgetting her are offered as the same act, and மறவா நம்மே sets her constancy against his.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched tract of dead trees is paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: நம் காதலர் and நம்மே are the woman speaking with the friend

320.reading: The woman says the man who brought her an unending hard sickness has gone by the forked hard track where the wind, stirred by roaring heat, lifts the bright clustered flowers of the thorny-trunked silk-cotton and scatters them on the earth like embers struck from the sky by thunder.
320.nuance: The flowers do not simply glow; they fall like thunder-struck embers, so the beauty of the path is turned into a rain of fire, matching the sickness without end (தவலில் அருநோய்) he has left her.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowering silk-cotton of the scorched track belongs to paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (செலவுப் பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the sickness is hers and the man is spoken of in the third person

links.note: Ainkurunuru 311 has the woman ask whether the man who crossed the forest will stay long (நீடுவர் கொல்); in Akananuru 69 the friend, by its colophon, comforts the woman who fears his delay with the answer that he will not stay long (நீடலர்) though he crossed the Mauryan cut.
links.teaches: The four-line poem gives only the woman's question and the long poem only the friend's answer, so together they show that the paalai exchange turned on a single verb of delay, asked in one mouth as a fear and returned in the other as a promise.

links.note: Both blessings are said by the woman to a thing of nature that governs her sight of the man who has left: the Kural blesses the moon on condition that it not set (படாஅதி வாழி மதி); Ainkurunuru 312 blesses the hill that has already hidden him (மறைத்த குன்றே).
links.teaches: The Kural's blessing is a bargain for sight, while the Sangam woman blesses the hill after it has hidden him, so her wish can only be for what the hill will do to him on the way, which shows the blessing turning from her own need to his safety.

links.note: In both the woman's heart has followed the man who left (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய்; இறந்தோர் தேஎத்துச் சென்ற நெஞ்சம்); the Kural calls it a fool, Ainkurunuru 317 asks the friend why it is so slow to come back.
links.teaches: The Kural judges the heart's going as folly, but the Ainkurunuru woman takes the going for granted and worries about the heart's delay, so the same flight of the heart becomes, in the older poem, a second absence that mirrors the man's.

links.note: Both state the same sign of separation on the same body part: the broad shoulders (பணைத்தோள்; பணைநீங்கி) waste and the bangles slip once the partner is gone.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the slipping bangle as a plain effect of the partner's absence, while the Ainkurunuru woman names the departed men as those who killed her longing, so the poem shows the bodily sign being used as an accusation, which the couplet's general statement leaves out.

links.note: Both turn on the woman's own inability to forget (மறப்பறியேன்; மறவா நம்மே); the Kural asks what would become of her if she forgot, Ainkurunuru 319 asks whether he has forgotten her.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps the question inside her (remembering burns, forgetting would kill), while the Sangam poem turns the same constancy outward into a charge against him, so read together they show the two directions the claim 'I do not forget' could be pointed.

links.note: In both a woman left behind speaks of a man who crossed the hills where the silk-cotton blooms: Akananuru 185 compares the leafless ilavam in flower to the lamps of a great festival (பெருவிழா விளக்கம் போல), Ainkurunuru 320 compares its falling flowers to embers struck by thunder (உருமுப்படு கனலின்).
links.teaches: The same flowering tree on the paalai road is a festival of lamps in one woman's mouth and a thunderbolt's embers in the other's, so the silk-cotton was not a fixed sign of danger but a vehicle that swung with the charge each woman laid against her man, his iron will in one and the endless sickness he gave in the other.

links.note: Both are the woman's complaint that ends on almost the same closing line (கோடுயர் பிறங்கல் மலை இறந் தோரே; நிலையுயர் பிறங்கல் மலைஇறந் தோரே) after naming her wasted broad shoulders (பணைத்தோள்) and slipping bangles.
links.teaches: The five-line decade poem is the bare frame of the thirteen-line Akananuru poem, the body's signs followed by the closing formula of the men who crossed the high hills, so the pair shows how a long paalai poem was built by filling the road between those two fixed ends with a scene.

source_issues: 311-320: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade (செலவுப் பத்து), so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.
312: என்னை may be 'my man' or 'my father'; the speaker (the woman left behind, or the girl in flight) turns on it.

314: line 2 reads கர்ங்கண் காக்கையொடு, a misprint for கருங்கண் (dark-eyed); the karu form is taken from காக்கையொடு. Line 1 (அவிர்தொடி கொட்பக் கழுதுபுகவு அயர) is obscure: whose bangles whirl is not clear.
315: line 3 (விழைநெகிழ் செல்லல் உறீஇ) is hard to construe; the reading 'a sorrow that undoes what she cherished' is tentative.
319: line 2 மண்புரை is taken as cracked or heaped earth; the sense is not certain.
